article.headline: The PEG Paradox: Why the Semiconductor Sector's Cheapest Names May Also Be Its Most Obvious
article.lede: A ranking of thirty semiconductor giants by forward PEG ratio — a metric dividing next-year earnings multiples by projected earnings growth — reveals something the headline valuations conceal: several of the sector's most storied names are priced as though their earnings supercycle has already ended.
article.body:
The table that @bubbleboi circulated arranges thirty semiconductor companies by forward P/E (the price an investor pays today per dollar of next-year earnings) and then divides that multiple by the expected EPS growth rate to produce a forward PEG ratio. A PEG below 1.0 conventionally signals that the market is not fully compensating investors for the growth embedded in consensus estimates — in other words, the stock is cheap relative to what it is expected to earn. By that standard, the top of this list is extraordinary. SK Hynix trades at 4.3 times next-year earnings against 23% expected EPS growth, yielding a PEG of 0.18. Micron, the American memory incumbent, sits at 5.4x on nearly 70% projected EPS growth, producing a PEG of 0.08 — effectively a rounding error. These are not obscure micro-caps; SK Hynix and Micron together represent over $1.2 trillion in combined market capitalisation and form the backbone of the global high-bandwidth memory (HBM) supply chain that every AI accelerator depends upon.

The explanation for such depressed multiples is not a mystery; it is a memory cycle scar. DRAM and NAND flash markets are famously cyclical, prone to inventory gluts that crater prices and earnings within a matter of quarters. Investors who lived through the 2022–2023 downturn — when Micron's EPS swung from roughly $8 to deeply negative — apply a structural discount to memory names, treating their earnings as temporarily elevated rather than durably compounding. The irony is that 2026 looks nothing like prior troughs: SK Hynix reported Q1 2026 revenue up 198% year-on-year, HBM capacity is reportedly fully committed through the year, and Morgan Stanley lifted its 2026 and 2027 earnings forecasts for SK Hynix by 56% and 63% respectively. The market's cyclical discount persists even as the cycle itself may be structurally different — one driven by AI infrastructure demand that carries longer lead times and stickier purchase commitments than the consumer electronics cycles of the past.

NVIDIA occupies a fascinating position in the middle of the table. At 17.5x forward earnings on 34.8% projected EPS growth, its PEG of 0.50 places it among the cheapest large-cap technology franchises on the planet — cheaper on this measure than Applied Materials, TSMC, Broadcom, or any of the semiconductor equipment names. The company delivered $216 billion in fiscal-year revenue for FY2026, up 65% year-on-year, and its hyperscaler customers — Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta — have collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capital expenditure for 2026 alone. That NVIDIA's forward multiple has compressed to 17x reflects the market's growing uncertainty about whether current spending levels are sustainable rather than any deterioration in the underlying franchise.

At the other end of the spectrum, ARM Holdings stands in a category of its own: 98.5x next-year earnings against only 21% projected EPS growth yields a PEG of 4.67 — the most expensive name on the list by a wide margin, and a figure that GuruFocus placed even higher (above 110x) as of late April 2026. ARM's premium reflects the thesis that it is not merely a chip designer but the inevitable royalty collector of every compute device on earth, from smartphones to AI servers. That thesis may be correct, but at a PEG of 4.67, investors are paying for decades of future royalty streams today. Monolithic Power Systems (PEG 2.95) and Analog Devices (PEG 2.05) sit in similarly stretched territory, their defensive, industrial-facing revenue profiles commanding premium multiples that leave little room for earnings disappointment.

Two names deserve particular scrutiny for structural reasons. Intel's 101% projected EPS growth looks dramatic but is arithmetically trivial to achieve: it is bouncing off a near-zero earnings base following years of execution stumbles and the $7 billion charge associated with its foundry restructuring under successive CEOs. Q1 2026 delivered $13.6 billion in revenue with non-GAAP EPS of $0.29 — a genuine beat against a consensus that had modelled something close to breakeven — and the data-centre division grew 22%, but the 101% growth figure tells an investor almost nothing about whether Intel's normalised earnings power justifies its $500 billion valuation. Marvell presents a mirror image problem: the table shows 0.2% next-year EPS growth against a 42.1x forward multiple, rendering its PEG not-meaningful. Yet Marvell's fiscal 2026 non-GAAP EPS grew 81% year-on-year, suggesting that the near-zero growth figure reflects a specific transitional period rather than secular stagnation — Marvell's custom silicon and AI networking revenue continues to compound, even if the consensus has yet to catch up.

The broader picture the table draws is one of profound bifurcation. Memory companies trade as though the AI supercycle is a blip; royalty and IP-driven models like ARM trade as though their moat is infinite and already fully monetised. The most interesting opportunities, if the table is taken at face value, sit in the middle: NVIDIA, MediaTek (PEG 0.33), Broadcom (PEG 0.42), AMD (PEG 0.51), and Microchip Technology (PEG 0.49) all combine meaningful scale with forward PEGs well below 1.0, suggesting that the market is either underestimating their earnings durability or overestimating the risks to their growth trajectories. Whether "still so early" describes the AI infrastructure build-out, the market's repricing of that build-out, or simply the memory cycle's second innings is a question the table poses but cannot answer.

concepts.definition: The Price/Earnings-to-Growth ratio using forward (next fiscal year) estimates: forward P/E divided by next-year expected EPS growth rate. A PEG below 1.0 is conventionally considered inexpensive relative to growth; above 1.0 suggests the market is paying a premium for each unit of expected earnings expansion.

The price-to-earnings multiple calculated using next fiscal year's consensus earnings estimate rather than trailing reported earnings. It reflects what investors are willing to pay today for each dollar of expected future profit, and is the standard valuation shorthand for growth-stage technology and semiconductor companies.

A stacked DRAM architecture that delivers far greater data throughput per watt than conventional memory, and is the primary memory type used in AI accelerators like NVIDIA's H100 and B200. SK Hynix and Micron are the leading HBM suppliers, with SK Hynix currently holding the largest share of NVIDIA allocations.

Year-over-year percentage change in earnings per share. In cyclical industries like semiconductors, EPS growth rates can be dramatically distorted by the base period — a company recovering from a loss year can show triple-digit growth even with modest absolute earnings improvement.

article.fact_check: Intel's 101% projected EPS growth is a base-effect artifact: the company was near breakeven in fiscal 2025 after restructuring charges, so even a modest return to profitability produces a large percentage gain. Q1 2026 EPS came in at $0.29 non-GAAP vs. near-zero consensus, and full-year 2026 estimates range from $0.48–$0.56, making the 101% figure plausible but largely uninformative about normalised earning power. Marvell's 0.2% next-year EPS growth (N.M. PEG) contrasts sharply with its fiscal 2026 non-GAAP EPS growth of 81% — the flat consensus likely reflects a transitional quarter or fiscal-year boundary effect rather than a business plateau; Marvell's data-centre revenue reached 74% of total sales driven by AI networking ASICs. QUALCOMM's negative EPS growth (-0.3%) reflects the expected partial loss of Apple modem revenue as Apple transitions to in-house chips, partially offset by record automotive revenue ($1.3B in Q2 FY2026, +38% YoY). ARM's forward P/E of 98.5x in this table aligns with third-party estimates ranging from 90x to 121x as of April–May 2026 depending on methodology.

ticker_mu.name: Micron Technology, Inc.
ticker_mu.blurb: Micron is the only US-headquartered manufacturer of DRAM and NAND memory at scale, competing with Samsung and SK Hynix. Historically the most cyclical of the three, it has spent the past two years repositioning toward high-bandwidth memory (HBM), the stacked DRAM that pairs with AI accelerators, where pricing is multiples of standard DDR5 and contracts are multi-year rather than spot.
ticker_mu.recent: In March 2026 Micron began mass production of HBM4 12-Hi 36GB stacks for Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform; management has stated 2026 HBM capacity is sold out under binding agreements. Fiscal Q2 2026 revenue was around $23.9 billion, with non-GAAP gross margin near 75%. The board approved a 30% dividend increase and roughly $25 billion of fiscal-2026 capex. Despite a strong year-to-date move, the forward P/E remains in the high single digits on consensus, reflecting residual cyclicality scepticism.

ticker_qcom.name: QUALCOMM Incorporated
ticker_qcom.blurb: QUALCOMM is the dominant designer of smartphone application processors (Snapdragon) and the world leader in mobile baseband modems — the chips that connect phones to cellular networks. The company operates a dual business model: QCT (chip sales) and QTL (technology licensing), with the latter generating high-margin royalties on every 3G/4G/5G handset sold globally. QUALCOMM is actively diversifying into automotive silicon and edge AI processors to reduce dependence on the handset market, particularly following Apple's decision to develop its own modems.
ticker_qcom.recent: Q2 FY2026 revenue reached $10.6 billion with non-GAAP EPS of $2.65. Automotive revenue hit $1.3 billion (+38% YoY), crossing $5 billion annualised for the first time. The expected partial loss of Apple modem business is weighing on forward EPS consensus, producing near-flat EPS growth estimates (-0.3%) for next fiscal year despite strong automotive and IoT momentum. Forward P/E sits at ~15.7x — undemanding for a franchise with durable licensing revenue.

ticker_nxpi.name: NXP Semiconductors N.V.
ticker_nxpi.blurb: NXP Semiconductors is a Dutch-American chip designer specialising in automotive semiconductors, industrial microcontrollers, and secure connectivity. It is the largest automotive semiconductor supplier globally by revenue, with chips embedded in powertrain systems, ADAS (advanced driver assistance), vehicle networking (CAN/LIN/Ethernet), and EV battery management. NXP also produces i.MX applications processors and S32 automotive compute platforms. The company was spun out of Philips in 2006 and is headquartered in Eindhoven.
ticker_nxpi.recent: NXP has navigated automotive inventory corrections that pressured the sector in 2024–2025. A recovery in automotive chip demand is underpinning 20.9% forward EPS growth estimates for the next fiscal year. The company trades at a forward P/E of ~17.4x with a PEG of 0.83 — reasonable for a business with deep automotive design-win moats and long product lifecycle revenue. NXP is investing in software-defined vehicle platforms as OEMs consolidate their supplier relationships.

sources.title: Undervalued Semiconductor Stocks 2026 — AInvest

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.

ticker_2454-tw.name: MediaTek Inc.
ticker_2454-tw.blurb: MediaTek Inc. is a Taiwanese fabless semiconductor company that designs system-on-chip (SoC) solutions for mobile devices, smart TVs, networking, and IoT. It is one of the world's largest chip designers, competing with Qualcomm in the smartphone processor market. The company also supplies chips for AI, automotive, and edge computing applications.
ticker_2454-tw.recent: In the past 30 days, MediaTek's stock traded near its 52-week high of TWD 3,470, reflecting strong demand for its smartphone and AI chips. The company has been gaining market share in mid-range 5G chipsets and expanding into automotive and AI edge computing. No major earnings or news were reported in the last month.

ticker_tsmc.name: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited
ticker_tsmc.blurb: TSMC is the world's largest dedicated semiconductor foundry — a contract manufacturer that makes chips for fabless designers like NVIDIA, Apple, AMD, and QUALCOMM using its own process technology. It operates the most advanced production nodes on earth, including 3nm and 2nm, with N2 (2nm) entering high-volume production in 2025. TSMC manufactures an estimated 90%+ of the world's most advanced logic chips and is a structural chokepoint in the global semiconductor supply chain. The company is expanding manufacturing into the United States (Arizona fabs), Japan (Kumamoto), and Germany (Dresden).
ticker_tsmc.recent: TSMC reported record revenue throughout 2025–2026, driven by AI accelerator demand from NVIDIA and Apple silicon. Q1 2026 revenue rose approximately 42% YoY. Forward P/E stands at ~21.8x on 25% projected EPS growth (PEG 0.87) — modest relative to its monopolistic position in advanced logic. Arizona fab yields have improved significantly, addressing earlier concerns about cost competitiveness outside Taiwan.

ticker_ifnny.name: Infineon Technologies AG
ticker_ifnny.blurb: Infineon Technologies is a global power-semiconductor leader headquartered in Munich, Germany, trading on US markets as an ADR (IFNNY). Its product lineup for AI server power delivery includes OptiMOS and CoolMOS MOSFETs, high-density quad-phase power modules (OptiMOS TDM2454xx, 280A in a 10x9mm footprint), XDP digital hot-swap and protection controllers for 48V AI racks, EiceDRIVER isolated gate drivers supporting SiC and GaN topologies, and high-voltage GaN reference designs for LLC converters running at 800V input. Infineon is a preferred power-silicon partner in NVIDIA's 800V HVDC reference architecture for next-generation AI data centres.
ticker_ifnny.recent: Infineon closed FY2025 (ending September 2025) with revenue of €14.66 billion and significantly raised its AI power revenue target to approximately €1.5 billion in FY2026, citing rapidly rising AI infrastructure demand. Revenue for the quarter ending December 2025 was $4.26 billion, up 16.8% year-over-year. In Q1 FY2026 the company announced new HV GaN reference designs for AI server power architectures and expanded its XDP digital protection family with the XDP711-001 48V hot-swap controller. A new Smart Power Fab in Dresden is on track to open in summer 2026. FY2026 guidance calls for moderate total revenue growth, with AI power as the primary growth driver against softer automotive and industrial demand, and adjusted gross margin in the low-forties percent range.

ticker_avgo.name: Broadcom Inc.
ticker_avgo.blurb: Broadcom is a diversified semiconductor and infrastructure software company formed through a series of acquisitions, most recently VMware (closed 2023). Its chip portfolio spans networking ASICs (custom chips for hyperscaler AI clusters), enterprise storage controllers, WiFi silicon, and set-top-box processors. Broadcom's AI networking chips — particularly its Tomahawk Ethernet switching ASICs and custom AI accelerators built for Google, Meta, and Apple — have made it a second-tier AI infrastructure beneficiary behind NVIDIA. The VMware acquisition added high-margin enterprise software revenue that meaningfully improved the company's margin profile.
ticker_avgo.recent: Broadcom's FY2026 revenue (ending Oct 2026) is on track to exceed $65 billion, with AI-related chip revenue growing rapidly as hyperscalers expand custom silicon programs. Forward EPS growth of 56.3% and a forward P/E of ~23.4x produce a PEG of 0.42 — among the best risk-adjusted valuations in large-cap technology. CEO Hock Tan has guided to $60–90 billion in AI chip revenue by 2027 from three major hyperscaler customers alone.

ticker_amat.name: Applied Materials, Inc.
ticker_amat.blurb: Applied Materials is the world's largest semiconductor equipment company by revenue, supplying deposition, etch, ion implantation, and metrology tools used in chip fabrication at every major foundry and memory manufacturer. Unlike ASML (which focuses on lithography), Applied Materials covers the broadest range of wafer processing steps — most chips manufactured anywhere pass through multiple Applied Materials tools. The company also supplies solar and display manufacturing equipment. Its services business (AGS) provides recurring revenue through parts, upgrades, and maintenance contracts.
ticker_amat.recent: Applied Materials has benefited from sustained semiconductor equipment investment across logic (TSMC, Samsung, Intel), DRAM, and NAND capacity expansions. Forward P/E of ~27.3x on 27.1% projected EPS growth yields a PEG of 1.01 — right at the conventional fair-value boundary. Revenue for FY2025 exceeded $28 billion. U.S. export restrictions on advanced equipment to China have created some demand uncertainty but also pushed customers to accelerate domestic tool installations.

ticker_snps.name: Synopsys, Inc.
ticker_snps.blurb: Synopsys is the market leader in EDA (electronic design automation) — the software toolchains used by chip designers to design, simulate, verify, and synthesise integrated circuits before they are sent to a foundry for fabrication. Without EDA tools, modern chip design at sub-10nm nodes is effectively impossible. Synopsys also sells silicon intellectual property (IP) — pre-designed circuit blocks like USB controllers and PCIe interfaces that chip designers license and integrate. Its duopoly with Cadence Design Systems gives both companies enormous pricing power and sticky customer relationships.
ticker_snps.recent: Synopsys is in the process of acquiring Ansys, a simulation software company, in a deal valued at approximately $35 billion. Forward P/E of ~28x on 18.3% projected EPS growth yields a PEG of 1.53 — modestly expensive relative to its growth rate but reflective of the structural indispensability of EDA tools in an era of accelerating chip complexity. AI-driven chip design is increasing demand for Synopsys tools as companies attempt more complex designs on tighter schedules.

ticker_adi.name: Analog Devices, Inc.
ticker_adi.blurb: Analog Devices is one of the two largest analog semiconductor companies in the world (alongside Texas Instruments), with deep expertise in signal-chain ICs, data converters, and — critical for AI servers — power-management products including hot-swap controllers, multiphase voltage regulators, power-system management ICs (PSMICs), and DC-DC power stages. ADI's LTC4284/4286/4287 hot-swap family protects 48V AI rack infrastructure, while its MAX20790 and related multiphase controllers regulate power to GPUs and accelerators at the point-of-load. The company is also a leading supplier of 800 VDC first-stage conversion solutions designed to NVIDIA's high-voltage DC reference architecture for AI factories.
ticker_adi.recent: ADI reported Q1 FY2026 (quarter ending January 2026) EPS of $2.46 versus the $2.31 consensus, with revenue of $3.16 billion supported by a 50% year-over-year increase in data-centre revenue. AI and data-centre exposure now accounts for roughly one-fifth of total revenues. Q2 FY2026 guidance was set at $3.5 billion (±$100 million), with non-GAAP EPS of $2.88 (±$0.15) and adjusted operating margin of ~47.5%. In August 2025 ADI announced its first 800 VDC hot-swap and first-stage power solutions targeting NVIDIA intelligent platform management, with >98% conversion efficiency. The company has seen accelerating adoption of 48V/54V intermediate-bus converters and smart power stages for vertical power delivery in AI racks.

ticker_asml.name: ASML Holding N.V.
ticker_asml.blurb: ASML is a Dutch semiconductor equipment company and the sole manufacturer of EUV (extreme ultraviolet) lithography machines — the tools required to print the finest circuit features on leading-edge chips at 5nm and below. Every AI accelerator, high-bandwidth memory chip, and advanced logic die manufactured at TSMC, Samsung, or Intel passes through ASML optics. The company's monopoly position emerged after decades of public-private R&D investment in partnership with European governments and chipmakers.
ticker_asml.recent: ASML reported €32.7 billion in total net sales for full-year 2025, up roughly 16% year-on-year, with net income of €9.6 billion and a gross margin of 52.8%. Year-end backlog stood at €38.8 billion. Q4 2025 saw record total net sales of €9.7 billion, including revenue recognized for the first High-NA EUV systems — the next-generation machines required for 2nm nodes and below. TSMC accounts for an estimated 40% of EUV tool deliveries. ASML guides to €34–39 billion for 2026 and €44–60 billion by 2030 as High-NA adoption widens. In December 2025 Huawei and Chinese startup SiCarrier confirmed a functional EUV light source using an alternative plasma architecture, but analysts place production-ready Chinese competition no earlier than 2028–2030.

ticker_8035-t.name: Tokyo Electron Limited
ticker_8035-t.blurb: Tokyo Electron Limited develops, manufactures, and sells semiconductor production equipment globally. It offers coaters/developers, plasma etch systems, cleaning systems, deposition systems, test systems, and other products. The company is a leading player in the semiconductor equipment industry, serving markets in Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, China, North America, and Europe.

The company reported strong earnings on April 30, 2026, with net income up 5.6% year-over-year. The stock has gained over 140% in the past year.

ticker_amd.name: Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.
ticker_amd.blurb: AMD is a fabless semiconductor company that designs CPUs (EPYC for data centres, Ryzen for consumer PCs) and GPUs (Instinct for AI/HPC, Radeon for gaming and workstations). Under CEO Lisa Su, AMD has taken significant data-centre CPU market share from Intel with its EPYC server processors, which now command an estimated 30%+ of the x86 server CPU market. AMD's MI300X and MI350 AI accelerators compete directly with NVIDIA's H100/H200 family and are gaining traction with hyperscalers seeking GPU supply alternatives. All AMD chips are manufactured by TSMC.
ticker_amd.recent: AMD reported strong 2025 revenue growth led by EPYC and Instinct, with data-centre revenue crossing $12 billion annually. Forward P/E of ~32.6x on 63.8% projected EPS growth yields a PEG of 0.51 — compelling for a company with clear data-centre CPU momentum and an AI accelerator portfolio that is gaining customer adoption. NVIDIA's dominant CUDA ecosystem remains the primary competitive barrier for AMD's GPU ambitions.

ticker_mchp.name: Microchip Technology Incorporated
ticker_mchp.blurb: Microchip Technology is a leading supplier of 8/16/32-bit microcontrollers and analog semiconductors, with a deep power-management portfolio covering PMICs, LDO regulators, DC-DC controllers, gate drivers for MOSFETs and IGBTs, and SiC gate drivers under its mSiC brand. It is one of the largest suppliers of mixed-signal and connectivity ICs for industrial, automotive, aerospace, and data-centre applications. Its Digitally Enhanced Power Analog (DEPA) controllers and 600V gate driver families address the high-voltage side of AI server power delivery, while its broad PMIC lineup targets point-of-load regulation for FPGAs, MPUs, and ASICs in compute racks.
ticker_mchp.recent: Microchip reported Q3 FY2026 (quarter ending December 2025) net sales of $1.186 billion, up 15.6% year-over-year and beating guidance, with non-GAAP EPS of $0.44 against a $0.39 consensus. CEO Steve Sanghi cited broad-based recovery across end markets, non-GAAP gross margins expanding from 52% to 60.5%, and strong bookings building into the March 2026 quarter. Q4 FY2026 guidance was set at $1.26 billion (midpoint), representing roughly 30% year-over-year growth, with EPS of $0.48–$0.52. The company also introduced a new 600V gate driver family and the MCP16701 PMIC targeting AI, high-performance computing, and data-centre applications in early 2026.

ticker_klac.name: KLA Corporation
ticker_klac.blurb: KLA Corporation is the global leader in process control and yield management equipment for semiconductor manufacturing — the tools that inspect wafers and detect defects at every stage of chip fabrication. As process nodes shrink and pattern complexity increases, process control becomes more critical: a single undetected defect layer can ruin an entire wafer lot. KLA's near-monopoly in wafer inspection and metrology gives it unusually stable revenue even during equipment spending downturns, as chipmakers cannot defer defect inspection without catastrophic yield losses. KLA also supplies equipment for PCB, LED, and solar manufacturing.
ticker_klac.recent: KLA trades at a forward P/E of ~35.3x on 31.1% projected EPS growth, yielding a PEG of 1.14 — modest for a company with near-monopoly process control positioning. Revenue has grown steadily as the number of inspection steps per wafer increases with each new process node generation. KLA's recurring service revenue (parts, software) provides a stable base around which equipment revenue cycles.

ticker_002371-sz.name: NAURA Technology Group Co., Ltd.
ticker_002371-sz.blurb: NAURA Technology Group Co., Ltd. is a Chinese semiconductor equipment manufacturer specializing in etching, deposition, and cleaning equipment. The company is a key domestic supplier to China's semiconductor fabrication industry, benefiting from the country's push for self-sufficiency in chip manufacturing. It holds a leading market position in China for several semiconductor equipment categories.

ticker_txn.name: Texas Instruments Incorporated
ticker_txn.blurb: The largest pure-play analog-semiconductor maker in the world by revenue, with roughly twenty percent share of the analog market. Texas Instruments designs and manufactures power-management chips, signal-chain devices and embedded processors used in industrial machinery, automobiles and, increasingly, AI servers. Its strategy is unusual in the industry: it owns and operates several 300-millimetre wafer fabs in the United States, giving it a long-term cost advantage against fab-light competitors, but also requiring a multi-year capital-spending programme that compressed free cash flow through 2023-2024.
ticker_txn.recent: Q1 2026 revenue came in at $4.83 billion, ahead of the $4.53 billion consensus, with analog-segment revenue up 22 percent year on year and data-centre revenue up roughly 90 percent. Capital expenditure dropped 40 percent year on year to $676 million as the 300mm fab build-out tapers, and free cash flow rose to $1.40 billion. The company has also announced selective price increases of 15 to 85 percent on certain analog products effective April 2026, in line with similar moves by Analog Devices, Infineon and Murata. The stock is up roughly 50 percent year-to-date through April 2026.

ticker_lrcx.name: Lam Research Corporation
ticker_lrcx.blurb: Lam Research is a leading semiconductor equipment company specialising in deposition (CVD, ALD) and etch systems — the tools that add and remove material layers during chip fabrication. Lam has particularly strong positioning in 3D NAND flash memory manufacturing, where its multi-layer deposition and etch tools are essential for building the hundreds of memory layers in modern NAND stacks. It also supplies critical tools for DRAM and advanced logic. Lam competes most directly with Applied Materials and Tokyo Electron, with each company holding dominant positions in different tool categories.
ticker_lrcx.recent: Lam Research trades at a forward P/E of ~36.2x on 30.7% projected EPS growth (PEG 1.18). The company has benefited from the NAND memory capacity buildout and is positioned to grow as 3D NAND layer counts increase — requiring more of Lam's deposition cycles per wafer. Revenue exceeded $17 billion in FY2025. Export restrictions to China have created some headwinds but domestic and non-China customer spending has partially offset the impact.

ticker_mrvl.name: Marvell Technology, Inc.
ticker_mrvl.blurb: Marvell Technology is a fabless semiconductor company that designs custom AI silicon (XPUs) for hyperscalers, high-speed networking ASICs (application-specific integrated circuits) for data-centre switching, and storage controllers. Its custom silicon business — building proprietary AI accelerators for Google, Amazon, and Microsoft under long-term agreements — has become its fastest-growing segment. Marvell also supplies Ethernet SerDes (serialiser/deserialiser) components, optical DSPs for coherent networking, and enterprise storage chips. The company is headquartered in Santa Clara and manufactures exclusively at TSMC.
ticker_mrvl.recent: Marvell reported record FY2026 revenue of $8.2 billion, up 42% YoY, with data-centre revenue reaching 74% of total sales. Non-GAAP EPS of $2.84 represented 81% growth. Despite this, forward EPS growth estimates for the next fiscal year are near 0.2% — likely a fiscal-calendar base-effect or consensus lag — producing a non-meaningful PEG at a 42.1x forward P/E. Custom silicon revenue is expected to accelerate as hyperscaler XPU programs ramp into production.

ticker_ateyy.name: Advantest Corporation
ticker_ateyy.blurb: Advantest is a Japanese semiconductor test equipment company and the global leader in high-performance ATE (automated test equipment) for logic chips and memory. Its V93000 platform is the dominant tester for cutting-edge SoCs and AI accelerators; its T2000 family leads in DRAM and HBM test. As AI chips grow more complex and HBM stacks taller, the cost and time required for testing increases, directly benefiting Advantest's revenue per unit shipped. Advantest holds an estimated 50%+ share of the global ATE market for advanced logic and memory.
ticker_ateyy.recent: Advantest has ridden the AI and HBM supercycle. Demand for testing H100/H200/Blackwell GPUs and HBM3E modules has driven record orders. Forward P/E of ~42.7x on 40% projected EPS growth yields a PEG of 1.07 — essentially fair value for a monopoly-adjacent business in a structurally growing segment. Revenue is denominated largely in USD (test tool invoicing) but reported in JPY, creating currency translation effects.

ticker_cohr.name: Coherent Corp.
ticker_cohr.blurb: Coherent Corp. (formerly II-VI Incorporated, rebranded after the 2022 acquisition of Lumentum rival Coherent) develops and manufactures engineered materials, optoelectronic components, and laser systems across three segments: Networking, Materials, and Lasers. Its Networking segment — the primary AI data-center play — supplies indium-phosphide chips, transceiver modules, and silicon-photonics sub-assemblies to hyperscalers and networking OEMs. With roughly $5.8 billion in fiscal 2025 revenue, it is one of the largest vertically integrated photonics companies in the world.
ticker_cohr.recent: Coherent joined the S&P 500 in March 2026, the same month it announced general availability of the industry's first dual-laser QSFP28-DCO module — a compact form factor enabling 100G coherent transmission over a single fiber with up to 300 km reach. At OFC 2026 the company showcased an expanded InP portfolio including 400 mW CW lasers, 200G/400G photodiodes, and 800G/1.6T modulators. Fifteen analysts hold an average "Strong Buy" rating with a consensus 12-month price target near $278.

ticker_asx.name: ASE Technology Holding Co., Ltd.
ticker_asx.blurb: ASE Technology is the world's largest OSAT (outsourced semiconductor assembly and test) company, responsible for packaging and testing chips after they leave the foundry wafer fab. Chip packaging — the process of cutting wafers into individual dies, mounting them in substrates, and connecting them to the outside world — is increasingly strategic as advanced packaging (chiplets, CoWoS, SoIC) becomes essential for AI accelerators that exceed the reticle size limits of individual dies. ASE's CoWoS-compatible packaging capacity has become a key bottleneck in NVIDIA Blackwell GPU supply chains. ASE is headquartered in Kaohsiung, Taiwan.
ticker_asx.recent: ASE has benefited from surging demand for advanced packaging from AI chip supply chains. NVIDIA's Blackwell GPUs require CoWoS advanced packaging, a significant portion of which flows through ASE and its competitor SPIL (a subsidiary). Forward P/E of ~47.4x on 39.7% projected EPS growth yields a PEG of 1.19. Revenue growth is driven by advanced packaging volumes rather than legacy wire-bond assembly.

ticker_mpwr.name: Monolithic Power Systems, Inc.
ticker_mpwr.blurb: A fab-light analog company that designs high-density power-management integrated circuits — the chips that step a server's intermediate-bus voltage down to the sub-1-volt rail an AI accelerator actually consumes. MPWR moved from a broad-based analog supplier into the dominant provider of GPU-adjacent power modules during the H100 generation, displacing the incumbent Vicor at Nvidia. Its modules are characterised by very high current density and tight integration, which matter enormously as AI racks push past 100 kilowatts.
ticker_mpwr.recent: In early 2026, management raised the floor on its enterprise-data growth target to 50-percent-plus from a prior 30-to-40 percent range, citing acceleration in Nvidia Blackwell shipments. Analyst notes suggest MPWR may take roughly 70 percent of power-management sockets on the forthcoming Vera Rubin GPU platform (VR200 NVL144 and R200 HGX), potentially adding more than $100 million to 2026 estimates. The stock has gained roughly 90 percent over the trailing twelve months and trades near all-time highs, leaving the AI exposure largely in the price.

ticker_intc.name: Intel Corporation
ticker_intc.blurb: Intel is the world's largest semiconductor company by revenue (historically) and the only major chip company that both designs and manufactures its own processors at scale. Its product portfolio spans PC and server CPUs (Core, Xeon), AI accelerators (Gaudi), FPGAs (Altera), and networking silicon. Intel's foundry ambition — Intel Foundry Services (IFS), renamed Intel Foundry — aims to manufacture chips for external customers on its 18A and 14A process nodes, positioning the company as a Western alternative to TSMC. After CEO Pat Gelsinger was replaced in late 2024, the company has undergone significant restructuring.
ticker_intc.recent: Intel reported Q1 2026 revenue of $13.6 billion, up from a depressed base, with non-GAAP EPS of $0.29 versus a near-zero consensus — the beat sent shares up 20%+ in after-hours trading. Data-centre revenue grew 22% YoY. Full-year 2026 EPS estimates of $0.48–$0.56 would represent ~101% growth from the 2025 base — a base-effect figure that reflects restructuring charges and near-zero profitability rather than a dramatic business inflection. Intel trades at ~62.1x forward earnings with a PEG of 0.61 given the distorted growth denominator.

ticker_arm.name: Arm Holdings plc
ticker_arm.blurb: Arm Holdings licenses processor architectures and physical IP to virtually every chip company on earth. Rather than manufacturing chips, Arm charges royalties on every device that ships using an Arm-based design — from the iPhone to Android phones to embedded microcontrollers to, increasingly, cloud server chips and AI accelerators. Its v9 architecture is the basis for Apple Silicon, NVIDIA's Grace CPU, Amazon's Graviton, and the majority of mobile SoCs. Arm's business model is uniquely capital-light and royalty-compounding: as ASPs (average selling prices) of chips using Arm cores rise — driven by AI compute demand — Arm's royalty revenue grows without proportional cost increases.
ticker_arm.recent: Arm trades at a forward P/E of ~98.5x on only 21.1% projected EPS growth, producing a PEG of 4.67 — the most expensive name in a table of thirty large-cap semiconductor stocks. Third-party estimates place the forward P/E even higher (90–121x as of April 2026). The premium reflects the thesis that Arm is the royalty collector of the entire AI compute era, but at a PEG of 4.67, investors are pricing in decades of compounding that has not yet materialised.
